Sub Topic: Fire Results from all methods of IR calibration and the thermocouple show significant heating of the sample surface well ahead of the flame front. While results from the bandpass filter are limited by the minimum calibration temperature of 150 C, there is still a noticeable preheating region approximately 5 mm ahead of the flame front. Using the DRX with no filter captured lower temperatures than using the narrow bandpass filter. However, the preheating temperatures ahead of the flame front and peak temperatures behind the flame front differ significantly from the other test methods and thermocouple results. This suggests that emissions from the window tainted the temperature readings. Finally, using the DRX with the quartz disk allowed for the same lower temperatures as to be recorded. The preheating temperature trends are similar to the thermocouple, while the peak temperatures trends are similar to the results obtained with the narrow bandpass filter. Results from the thermocouple likely represent the true sample surface temperature for much of the preheating region.

However, the temperature recorded at the flame front by the thermocouple is 1095 C and is off scale in Figure 4. This is because as the flame front reaches the thermocouple, the sample material surrounding the thermocouple is removed. This leads to the thermocouple effectively reading a gas phase temperature. Results from the narrow bandpass filter, DRX with quartz disk, and the thermocouple all show similar results in the region approximately 2 mm ahead of the flame front where the temperature gradient is steepest. Each method is bound by physical limitations of the test setup, emissions and signal loss from the quartz window of the NCA for the IR measurements, and reading of gas phase temperatures for the thermocouple. Conclusions Data collected from the IR camera and thermocouples shows that significant forward heat conduction ahead of the flame front occurs on the surface during the tests. This was estimated using Fourier’s Law and a peak of 1.9 kW/m2 was found in the region 1 mm ahead of the flame. Addition of the quartz disk to the 3-5 micron lens with the DRX enabled significantly improved results in the preheating region. In progress work of cooling the quartz window of the NCA to further reduce emissions may bring the IR camera and thermocouple results further inline. Differences between the IR camera and thermocouple in the flame region can be attributed to the thermocouple reading the gas phase temperature. Ultimately, the measurements of forward heat conduction demonstrate the need to model all further tests of PMMA in the NCA as a two-dimensional problem.

ACME BRE (PSI-20), Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator. Pillar: prevention. Hardware: ACME in CIR. Summary: The Burning Rate Emulator used porous circular gas burners, 25 mm and 50 mm across, to imitate burning solid fuels in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the International Space Station. Methane and ethylene mixed with nitrogen were burned in still air at several pressures and oxygen levels, including 21% at 14.7 psia, 26.5% at 10.2 psia and 34% at 8.2 psia. Carbon dioxide ambients and extinction limits were also planned. The record says quasi-steady burning was observed without airflow, notably in elevated-oxygen atmospheres. Interpretation: relevant to burning without ventilation, since cutting airflow is a standard step in putting out spacecraft fires, but the burner stands in for solids. Summary: ACME CFI-G studied cool diffusion flames, which burn at low temperature, using gas fuels on spherical porous burners in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the International Space Station. Planned fuels were propane, n-butane and n-pentane, with normal and inverse flames and many reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures. Cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes and thermocouples observed the flames, and CFD and kinetics modeling support the tests. Images from the BASS and BASS-II experiments were processed with new two-color tomography using DSLR cameras to reconstruct soot and temperature fields for comparison. Model checks included flame geometry, temperature, soot volume fraction and flame spread rate, with focus on the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone. The stated aim is a screening tool for material flammability limits. The record gives no numerical results. Interpretation: a model built on BASS data, not new experiments. FLEX (PSI-69), Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Pillar: suppression. Hardware: MDCA in CIR. Summary: FLEX burned large liquid fuel droplets, about 3 mm for the basic tests, in the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus on the International Space Station. Its main goal was to find the Limiting Oxygen Index, the lowest oxygen level that sustains a flame, as a function of pressure (0.5 to 1.5 atm) and to see how gaseous suppressants such as carbon dioxide, helium and SF6 change it. It also measured burning rates, extinction behavior, radiation, soot and temperature. The hypothesis is that missing buoyant flow changes flammability limits and suppressant effectiveness. The record text gives no numerical results. Interpretation: strong on oxygen and suppressant limits for liquid fuels, not solids. Summary: SAFFIRE-I burned a large fabric sample, about 0.94 m by 0.4 m, inside an enclosure on a Cygnus cargo vehicle after it left the International Space Station. SAME (PSI-102), Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment. Pillar: detection. Hardware: Smoke instruments. Summary: SAME measured the smoke particles produced by overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity on the International Space Station. Crew set up hardware in the Glovebox, ran an igniter for 15 to 60 seconds, each event lasting about 2 minutes, and sampled smoke with thermophoretic probes. Particles were later examined with a transmission electron microscope, and two smoke detectors were checked. The hypothesis is that without buoyancy, smoke particles grow larger than in normal gravity. A prediction code and data for future spacecraft fire detectors were the stated aims. The record text gives no numerical results. Interpretation: smoke detection evidence, not flame spread. SAME data modeling (PSI-115), Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity. Pillar: detection. Hardware: Smoke instruments. Summary: This ground modeling study used numerical simulation to compare how smoke particles grow in microgravity and in Earth gravity. It simulated dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles from pyrolysis vapor released by a heated sample, in a geometry similar to the SAME experiments, using direct numerical simulation at two low cross-flow velocities. SLICE (PSI-106), Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment. Pillar: context. Hardware: MSG flow duct. Summary: SLICE studied the structure and stability of laminar gas diffusion flames in microgravity on the International Space Station. A fan-driven flow duct with exchangeable burner tubes and sensors was used with methane, ethylene and nitrogen-diluted mixtures, ignited manually in a controlled coflow of air. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were taken across 13 experiments. Goals included liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner sizes, the effect of nitrogen dilution on soot and stability, flame length and radiative heat loss, and validating models. The hypothesis is that burner diameter, coflow velocity and fuel composition strongly affect these flames. The record gives no numerical results. Interpretation: flame stability data with no solid fuels. Summary: SPICE looked for the smoke point, where a flame starts emitting soot, of laminar gas jet flames in microgravity inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the International Space Station. SPICE data analysis (PSI-60), Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets. Pillar: context. Hardware: Ground and modeling. Summary: This ground study reanalyzed SPICE images to understand why soot formation differs between normal-gravity and microgravity flames. More than 1,600 raw DSLR images were decoded and analyzed with color-ratio pyrometry to get soot temperature fields, then calibrated light measurements gave soot volume fractions. A soot model including radiation re-absorption and aggregate growth was run for Yale and ACME burner setups under normal and microgravity conditions. Comparisons guided tests of how sensitive the results are to model parameters. The hypothesis is that microgravity flames are longer, more diffuse, cooler and sootier. The record gives no numerical results. Interpretation: derived soot and temperature fields from SPICE, not new flame tests. Coverage of the Moon cabin condition in PSI. Of 1900 unified test rows, 808 record both oxygen fraction and total pressure and 254 of those also have an outcome label. In the cabin box (O2 >= 26% and total pressure <= 75 kPa) there are 17 rows, all from FLEX droplet tests, with 0 outcome labels. Solid-fuel rows (272) reach at most 22.722 percent O2 at 98.2853 to 102.208 kPa; 0 solid rows are at or above 24 percent O2.

Pressure scaling of the oxygen effect (theta; 1 means partial pressure of O2 governs, 0 means O2 mole fraction governs). FLEX droplet extinction diameter, n=158: theta = 0.285 (95 percent bootstrap interval 0.0515 to 0.626). CFI hot-flame extinction diameter, n=143: theta = 0.0728 (0.0376 to 0.109). Pure-N2 FLEX subset cannot identify theta (interval -10.9 to 1.87). Both responses are liquid-droplet extinction diameters, not solid-fuel flammability limits. FLEX pressure leverage rests on two clusters near 70 and 100 kPa; the pure-N2 subset cannot identify theta. CFI has two O2 levels (17 and 21 percent) and a helium-diluted subset, so its O2 exponent rests on one contrast. Bootstrap resamples rows as independent; repeated tests on one apparatus are not independent in fact. Applying theta to solid fuels is an assumption, labelled as such wherever it is used.
